quote: Elsewhere the chief priest of the Temple has James, "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", stoned.
heart: Josephus was a priest from Jerusalem who commanded the Jewish forces in Galilee when the Jews rose against Rome. In 67 he gave himself up to the Roman general Vespasian, and he spent the rest of his life at Rome, under the emperors' favour, writing his people's history (E1, E2, E6, S5; Documented, almost all from his own books). In his *Antiquities of the Jews*, finished about 93, he wrote a few lines each on John the Baptist, on James "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", and on Jesus himself (E11–E14; the John and James lines Widely Accepted as his). Christians kept and quoted those lines for centuries as a witness from outside the church. The passage on Jesus is the one they argued over. It has been disputed since the sixteenth century, an editor wrote in 1890 (EH-ed 9182–9185). Whether he wrote it as it stands is **Contested** (D2).

quote: served for a time as secretary to the emperor Hadrian, until Hadrian dismissed him
heart: Suetonius, a Roman scholar who wrote the lives of twelve of Rome's rulers, from Julius Caesar to Domitian, around 120, gives the Christians two short lines and no more. Under Claudius, he writes, the Jews were driven from Rome for rioting at the urging of "Chrestus"; under Nero, the Christians were punished as people of a new and harmful superstition (E1, E3: Documented as his words; the date of the book, S4: Dominant Modern Reconstruction). He is on the tree because these are among the very few outside notices of the first Christians at Rome, and readers still argue over who "Chrestus" was (I1, D1: Documented that they are read so; who Chrestus was, Contested).

quote: said the passage was open to challenge
heart: Tacitus, a Roman historian writing about fifty years after the great fire of Rome in 64, gives the fullest account outside the church of what Nero did to the Christians. Rumoured to have ordered the fire, Nero put the guilt on them and had a huge number killed as a public show. To explain their name, Tacitus adds that their founder, Christus, was executed under the emperor Tiberius by Pontius Pilate (M2–M6: Documented as Tacitus's account; the year 64, S1: Documented; the date he wrote, S3: Dominant Modern Reconstruction). He despised them and said so, and his one chapter became what later historians built on (M3, M4, M7, D4: Documented; I1: Documented).

quote: sentenced to be killed by wild animals in the arena
asks: Why was he arrested and sentenced, and by whom?
heart: Ignatius, bishop of the church at Antioch in Syria, was taken under armed guard across the Roman world to Rome, condemned to die by wild beasts in the arena (E1, E2, S6; Documented, his own words). On the road he wrote seven letters, most of them to churches that came out to meet him, and they are almost all we know of him (E3, D2; the letters Documented; "almost all we know" is McGiffert's judgement, Widely Accepted; that these seven are his, Widely Accepted, long disputed). Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, sent on the ones he held, and later writers quoted them (I1, I2–I4; Documented).

quote: he has to sail suddenly from Troas
heart: Ignatius, bishop of the church at Antioch in Syria, was taken under armed guard across the Roman world to Rome, condemned to die by wild beasts in the arena (E1, E2, S6; Documented, his own words). quote: A philosopher at Rome, he adds, tried to have both Justin and him put to death.
asks: Why did he want them killed?
heart: Tatian, a man born "in the land of the Assyrians" and trained in Greek learning, became a Christian at Rome and a hearer of Justin. In his *Address to the Greeks* he turned on everything he had studied: their gods, their philosophers and their arts, all borrowed, he said, from the peoples they called barbarians, and all younger than Moses (S2, E3, E5; Documented, his own words). After Justin's death he broke with the church, by the account of his opponent Irenaeus, about 172 by Eusebius's date (E6, S4; Documented as Irenaeus's account and Eusebius's date). He went back east, and his *Diatessaron*, the four Gospels woven into one continuous story, became for about two centuries the gospel most Syriac-speaking churches heard read (E7, E8, I1; the journey east Widely Accepted, resting on Epiphanius two centuries later; the harmony's use Documented; "very widely if not universally read" is Hogg's judgment, Widely Accepted).

quote: In 235 he was exiled to Sardinia with Pontianus, the bishop of Rome.
asks: Why were they exiled, and by whom?
heart: Hippolytus was a Greek-writing teacher and elder of the church at Rome in the early two hundreds (S1, S2; Documented). In his *Refutation of All Heresies*, written after 222, he attacked Callistus, bishop of Rome from 217, as a man who forgave sinners too easily and who shared the teaching that Father and Son were one and the same (E4, E6, E7, E9; Documented as his charge; what Callistus taught, Contested). In 235 he was sent into exile on the island of Sardinia together with Pontianus, the bishop of Rome (E11; Documented, the list of 354; that the exile is this Hippolytus, Widely Accepted; that he was set to work in the mines is the historians' reading, DUH 11685–11686, EUS 35698–35700). Whether he led a rival church against the bishops of Rome is disputed (D2; Contested).

quote: a bishop of Rome took their churches and drove their bishop into private houses
asks: Why did Rome's bishop do this?
heart: Novatian was a leading elder of the church at Rome and a writer on the faith; his *On the Trinity* set out what the church believed of Father, Son and Spirit (E2; the book Documented; "leading" Widely Accepted, from Cornelius's sneer and Harnack, E2, E5). In 251 a stricter party made him a rival bishop of Rome against Cornelius, and he led a church that would not take back to communion those who had denied the faith under persecution; it left their pardon to God (E5, E8; Documented). That church lasted for centuries, and almost all we know of him comes from the men who fought him (S3, I1, I2; Witness kinds; Documented).

quote: In 257 the governor sent Cyprian away.
heart: Pontius, Cyprian of Carthage's deacon, went with him into exile in 257 by choice, and was with him on his last night in 258 (E2, E6; Documented, the book's own claims; his name and his office are Jerome's, E1). Soon after, he wrote *The Life and Passion of Cyprian*, so that Cyprian's example would reach later generations (E8; Documented, his own words; written about 259, Dominant Modern Reconstruction). It tells a bishop's life from his baptism to his death; a leading historian called it the oldest Christian biography that survives, and others call it a speech of praise (I3; Contested). The book is unsigned; Jerome, about 130 years later, gives the deacon's name (E1; Widely Accepted).

quote: the next day, 14 September 258, he was beheaded
asks: Why was Cyprian executed, on what charge?

quote: After his death the fellowship split
heart: Pachomius, in Upper Egypt in the fourth century, gathered hermits into shared monasteries under one written rule, and that rule reached the West through Jerome's Latin version.

quote: In 360 a synod at Constantinople deposed him again.
asks: Why was he deposed this time?
heart: Cyril of Jerusalem taught the people preparing for baptism through the forty days of Lent, in the great church beside Golgotha. He went through the creed line by line, and after Easter he explained the rites they had just been through. His lectures survive because some of his hearers took them down as he spoke, an old note in one copy says. As bishop he was driven from his city three times in the quarrels over Arius's teaching, and Jerusalem's way of making new Christians became a pattern that a pilgrim from the West wrote home about.

quote: Socrates says Constantine's son Constantius removed the bishop of Constantinople
heart: When Alexander of Alexandria put Arius out, Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, the city where the emperor lived, took up Arius's cause (SOC 2123-2126, 2381-2391). After a short exile that followed Nicaea, he led the bishops who drove Arius's opponents from their churches, and he died bishop of Constantinople (SOC 4662-4668, 5885-5890, 6175-6177). Nearly everything we know of him was written by his enemies (Source_Sheet §5.1). Documented.

quote: Later councils, from 680 to 787, listed Evagrius with Origen and Didymus as condemned at Constantinople in 553.
heart: Evagrius Ponticus, a gifted deacon at Constantinople, fled the city over a love affair and became a monk in the Egyptian desert, where he named the eight tempting thoughts that trouble a monk and taught that prayer is the mind's own work. Long after his death, councils named him with Origen among the condemned, yet monks in the Latin West and the Syriac East went on using what he taught.

quote: At once he shut the churches of the Novatians, a strict Christian group outside his own, and seized their goods.
heart: Cyril was bishop of Alexandria, the head of the church in Egypt's great city, from 412 to 444. He taught that Christ is one: God's own Son, whom the Bible calls the Word, was himself born of Mary as a man, so she may rightly be called Mother of God, the one who gave birth to God (E4: Documented, his own words). He led the attack on Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, which ended with a council of bishops at Ephesus in 431 removing Nestorius from office (E6: Documented). His twelve short statements of faith, each cursing those who denied it, and his phrase "one incarnate nature of God the Word", meaning one Christ, God become man and never divided, became the test of true faith for the churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia that later refused the Council of Chalcedon (I1, I2: Documented for Egypt and Syria; Armenia from the census Chalcedon text, I4). Chalcedon, the council of 451 that said Christ is known in two natures, fully God and fully human, also took his letters as a guide (I4: Documented).

quote: In 415 a Christian mob led by a church reader, who read Scripture aloud in services, killed the philosopher Hypatia.

heart: In 325 the emperor Constantine called bishops to Nicaea to settle whether the Son is God as the Father is; they condemned Arius and wrote a creed calling the Son "begotten, not made", of one being with the Father, though it divided the church for decades.

quote: Later emperors set the council aside
asks: Why did emperors set it aside?
heart: In 451 more than five hundred bishops at Chalcedon confessed one Christ, one person known in two natures, fully God and fully human, taking Leo's Tome as their guide; the Greek and Latin churches accepted it, while the churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia refused it and still stand apart.

quote: By his own account, "Satan stirred up a quarrel" between him and the head of the church, Babowai.
heart: Barsauma was bishop of Nisibis, a city on the border between the Roman and Persian empires, in the late 400s. In 484 he led a synod, a council of bishops, at Beth Lapat against the catholicos, the head of his own church, and later took it back in writing (E5, E8, E10; Documented, his own letters). Yet what his side stood for became the Church of the East's settled law: clergy, the church's ordained ministers, free to marry, allowed in 486 and, in 497, accepted from Beth Lapat "only on this point"; and Theodore of Mopsuestia, a Greek Bible teacher, as its sure guide, confirmed in 605 (E11, I2, I3; Documented, the church's own synods). Writers of the churches that broke with it remembered him as the man who set the Persian church apart (I4, I5; Documented as their hostile claims).

quote: Barsauma took back everything done at Beth Lapat, its rules included.

quote: Babai then drove out a gentle monk named Jacob, unjustly, Thomas says, and condemned him in writing.
asks: Why was Jacob driven out and condemned?
heart: For close to twenty years in the early 600s, the Persian king Khosrau would not let the Church of the East have a catholicos, the head of the whole church (S5; Documented as Thomas of Marga's account; length Contested, 17 to 20 years). In those years Babai, abbot (head) of the Great Monastery on Mount Izla near Nisibis, a monk and not a bishop, went round the church's monasteries for its senior bishops. He tested what the monks believed and drove out those the bishops judged heretics, people teaching what the church had condemned (E5; Documented as Thomas's account, about 840). He wrote the *Book of the Union*, on how Christ is one person who is both fully God and fully human, and his church kept and honoured his books (E6, I1; the books' keeping Documented; that his writing settled his church's teaching on Christ is the judgment of modern historians, Dominant Modern Reconstruction).

quote: Reccared had become Catholic in his first year as king.
asks: Why did the king turn Catholic?
heart: In 589 at Toledo, King Reccared and the Gothic bishops gave up their Arian church and joined the Catholic faith of their Roman subjects, cursing their old faith, taking its churches from it, and adding "and the Son" to the creed.

quote: he also attacked Origen's ordination by the bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem
asks: Why did he attack the ordination?
heart: Young Origen took a verse of Matthew literally and did a drastic deed to himself, which his bishop Demetrius first admired and later used against him.

quote: Origen's boldest ideas kept being read, loved and contested by turns
asks: Which ideas, and contested over what?
heart: Alexandria's Christians left a settled inheritance (the Nicene confession, sharing God's life, deeper Scripture reading) and a live argument over Origen.

quote: defended it through five exiles
asks: Why was he exiled, and by whom?
heart: From about 150 to 400, Alexandria's Christians passed on one faith through teachers and through worship, both centered on the Logos, and held to Nicaea as bishops took over the guarding of the creed.

quote: Origen's work was carried forward too, and people loved it and argued over it.
heart: From about 150 to 400, Alexandria's Christians passed on one faith through teachers and through worship, both centered on the Logos, and held to Nicaea as bishops took over the guarding of the creed.

quote: the wound of Sasima among it
asks: What was the wound of Sasima?
heart: Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus formed a deep friendship as students at Athens, which Gregory chose to remember first in his funeral speech for Basil.

quote: His family had been purged
heart: Emperor Julian, raised among Christians, barred Christian teachers from teaching the classics, striking at the learning Cappadocian leaders prized, and Gregory attacked him fiercely.

quote: taking measures against Caesarea itself
heart: Emperor Julian, raised among Christians, barred Christian teachers from teaching the classics, striking at the learning Cappadocian leaders prized, and Gregory attacked him fiercely.

quote: committed an offense
heart: Abba Moses, called to judge a brother's fault, carried a leaking basket of sand to show his own sins, and the brother was let go.

quote: In 400, a council at Alexandria condemned Origen and the monks who followed him.
asks: Why did the council condemn them?
heart: From about 320 to 430, Egyptian Christians left for the desert to give up everything, living alone or in communities, guided by wise elders and by Evagrius's system, until a dispute over God's body broke the movement's circle.

quote: In the end Marcellinus ruled against the Donatists
asks: Why did he rule that way?
heart: At the 411 conference in Carthage the Donatist bishops stood and argued their case before the imperial judge, who ruled against them.

quote: he was thrown from the cliff
heart: The Donatists' account of Marculus tells of his flogging, his vision, his fall from a cliff and his body's gentle landing.

quote: Tyconius wrote the Book of Rules.
asks: A book of rules about what?
heart: Tyconius's book outlived his party and shaped Augustine, while the Donatist contest lasted long after 439 with no line to any church today.

quote: A council of his own Donatist party is reported to have condemned him
heart: Tyconius's book outlived his party and shaped Augustine, while the Donatist contest lasted long after 439 with no line to any church today.

quote: and penal laws followed
heart: Two rival churches in North Africa split over whether a bishop's failure under persecution voided his acts; the Donatists saw themselves as the pure church, suffered state force, and lost at Carthage in 411.

quote: When the clergy at Condate fell to quarreling
heart: Martin made peace among quarreling clergy at Condate, died on sackcloth and ashes, and was mourned by thousands.

quote: his father informed on him
heart: Young soldier Martin cut his cloak in two for a freezing beggar, saw Christ wearing it, and was baptized.

quote: After Priscillian was put to death
asks: Who was Priscillian, why was he executed, and accused of what?
heart: At Trier Martin took communion with bishops he had refused, to save lives, and carried grief for it for the rest of his life.

quote: Martin once took communion with bishops he had refused, to save lives.
asks: Why had he refused them, and whose lives?
heart: Two Gallic monk households, Martin's at Tours and Cassian's and Lérins's in the south, each kept the monk's life inside the bishop's office while measuring themselves against Egypt.

quote: Marcella was the one who set in motion the condemnation of the heretics in Rome
asks: Which heretics, and condemned for what?
heart: Marcella, a Roman widow, pressed Jerome with hard scriptural questions and became an authority others consulted.

quote: Constantius had it removed, Julian put it back, and Gratian removed it again.
asks: Why did each emperor do this?
heart: Symmachus petitioned to restore the altar of Victory, Ambrose answered that a Christian state may not fund false worship, and the altar stayed removed.

quote: When Constantine stepped into the quarrel in Africa's church
heart: Constantine answered the Donatist quarrel by councils and by building a new church for the Catholics, not by force.

quote: Then he fell.
heart: Eutropius, who had ended the church's right of refuge, fled to the altar when he fell, and John preached on the emptiness of power.

quote: later he was exiled and executed
heart: Eutropius, who had ended the church's right of refuge, fled to the altar when he fell, and John preached on the emptiness of power.

quote: A council in the East had condemned Athanasius of Alexandria and removed him from office
heart: Julius of Rome answered an Eastern council's condemnation of Athanasius by claiming the custom was to write to Rome first, a custom others disputed.

quote: his letter, the Tome, was read to the assembled bishops
heart: At Chalcedon Leo's Tome was acclaimed, but the council raised Constantinople's rank and Leo refused it, insisting no royal city could be an apostolic see.

quote: The empire stopped hunting the church, and within a year toleration was law.
asks: Why did it stop, and what law, by whom?
heart: Eusebius reports Constantine's own account of a cross of light and a dream before the Milvian Bridge, after which the persecution ended.

quote: whole regions rejected it at once, starting in Egypt, at the council itself
heart: Chalcedon ended with lasting division, and its rival claims about Rome's primacy and Constantinople's rank are still argued.

heart: Luther, remembering years later, told how he went before Cardinal Cajetan in 1518, knelt, and refused to recant.

heart: Melanchthon's confession for the 1530 Diet was presented by princes and city councils, not Luther, as a summary of their teaching.

quote: to hear the quarrels over religion

quote: His 1543 treatise against the Jews is real and part of this history
heart: This account tells the Lutheran churches in their own time and does not carry forward later history or later communities' beliefs.

quote: In 1525 Luther wrote against the peasants' rising, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews.
heart: From 1517 to 1580 a reform grew out of Wittenberg around a frightened conscience comforted by God's promise, carried by Luther's stands, German worship, the catechism and the Augsburg Confession.

quote: he was condemned and sent under armed guard on the long road to Rome
asks: Condemned by whom, and for what?
heart: Ignatius wrote letters urging unity around one bishop and one eucharist while traveling under guard to Rome to die.

quote: one of his sons had Aggai's legs broken as he sat teaching in the church
heart: The story Edessa's church told of its own beginning: King Abgar wrote to Jesus, and Addai came after the ascension to heal him and convert the city.

heart: In 1549 Calvin went to Zurich to settle fears that the two churches taught different things about the Supper. The result was the Consensus Tigurinus.

quote: test Zwingli's case against Scripture
heart: In 1523 Zurich's council called a public disputation, and afterward ruled for the reform and ordered all priests to preach the same way.

heart: Myconius recounts the morning Zwingli rode out and, from reports, how he died on the battlefield.

quote: He was exiled to Strasbourg in 1538
heart: Zurich and Geneva built Reformed churches on Scripture from 1519 to 1650. They differed over church and state, shared their stance on the Supper, and held to election.

heart: In 177 the Christians of Lyon were killed, and the letter about it centers on the enslaved woman Blandina, who outlasted every torture.

quote: the archbishop's crude test of his humility at the ordination and Moses' unruffled answer
asks: What was the test, and what did he answer?
heart: Moses, a former slave and robber, became a monk and priest, known for the leaking basket and for staying to be killed by raiders.

quote: When he was deposed and exiled in 404
heart: Olympias, a rich widow and deaconess, funded the church, stood by Chrysostom, and was exiled for it.

quote: He was consulted on Chalcedon and wrote in its favor
heart: Simeon lived on a pillar, drew crowds, arbitrated disputes, and wrote to emperors and bishops.

quote: in 488 the Roman population of Noricum was evacuated to Italy under Odoacer's orders
heart: Severinus guided the Danube towns of Noricum through the Roman collapse until the population left.

quote: She moved her nuns against the monks' will

quote: John was briefly imprisoned by the Paduans
heart: In 1233 preachers moved city to city and won a general peace among Italian communes, which collapsed within months.

quote: Juliana herself was driven from Cornillon twice by a hostile prior and the townspeople
heart: Juliana's vision of a missing feast led, after her death, to Corpus Christi being extended to the whole church.

quote: where rulers began to suppress it by 1261
heart: In 1260 a penitential movement of public scourging for peace spread across Italy and beyond and left lasting confraternities.

quote: Bishops and communes joined in, then grew wary
heart: In 1399 white-clad pilgrims processed from city to city in penance and reconciled enemies.
